answer.label: Not his words — a paraphrase of a real Ted Williams argument
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox hitter & Marine aviator
answer.sourceLine: No book, article, interview or broadcast has ever been produced for this sentence, and Wikiquote parks it in the “Unsourced” list on its Ted Williams talk page. The argument, though, is genuinely his: in the opening pages of The Science of Hitting Williams makes the case that golf is the easier game and lands the jab that “there’s that golf ball, sitting right there for you to hit.” The circulating one-liner is that thought compressed and tidied by someone else.

source.heading: What Ted Williams actually put in print

docMeta.dd: None located — Wikiquote files it under “Unsourced”
With John Underwood. New York: Simon and Schuster, 1971 (LCCN 79139668)

source.excerpt: “Golf is the only sport where the ball doesn’t move until you hit it.” — no book, article, interview or broadcast has ever been produced for this sentence. What Williams did put in print, in the opening chapter of The Science of Hitting, is the same idea in his own rougher voice: golf asks nothing of your eyesight, your speed, your youth or your nerve, and “there’s that golf ball, sitting right there for you to hit.”
trail: Wikiquote catalogues the line on its Ted Williams talk page ↗, under a heading that reads simply “Unsourced” — the holding pen for lines nobody has been able to tie to a book, article or broadcast.
It is absent from the sourced Wikiquote article ↗, from Baseball Almanac’s Williams page ↗, and from ESPN Classic’s Williams quote collection ↗.
What he did publish is a different sentence, in the book the Library of Congress catalogues as The Science of Hitting, New York: Simon and Schuster, [1971] ↗, written with John Underwood.
He was no stranger to the comparison: Golf Digest’s July 1960 cover story ↗ runs under his byline, with Sam Snead writing the companion piece about him — but neither is the source of this line.
source.excerptNote: The clause is the last item in a list — Williams is answering the objection “what about golf?” to his opening claim that hitting a baseball is the single most difficult thing to do in sport. He goes on to call golf a fine game he does not mean to detract from, and names Sam Snead as a great athlete.

source.rightsNote: The circulating one-liner has no identifiable source, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it — an unsourced sentence cannot be declared public domain. The passage Williams actually published belongs to The Science of Hitting (Simon and Schuster, 1971), which is firmly in copyright; the short clause quoted here is used as a citation for provenance, not as a reproduction.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.kicker: About the man it is pinned on
author.heading: Ted Williams
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox hitter · Marine aviator
author.bio: Theodore Samuel Williams was the last man to bat .400 in a major-league season, hitting .406 for the Boston Red Sox in 1941, and he twice left the game in his prime to fly as a Marine aviator — in the Second World War and again in Korea. He was also the most articulate hitter who ever lived: The Science of Hitting, written with John Underwood, remains one of the game’s standard texts on the swing. His opinion of golf runs straight through its opening chapter — a fine game, he allowed, and a considerably easier one.

misattribution.heading: What is wrong, and what is right
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication invented out of nothing, and it is not a quotation either. It sits in the awkward middle: a real Ted Williams position, rewritten by an unknown hand into a sentence he is not documented as having spoken or written.

items.why: The sentence is catalogued only in the “Unsourced” section of Wikiquote’s Ted Williams talk page ↗. It is absent from the sourced Wikiquote article ↗ and from Baseball Almanac ↗, which prints a source line beside every quotation and flags its own uncited ones “Widely Attributed”.

He really did argue that golf is the easier game because the ball is not moving — in print, in the book the Library of Congress catalogues as The Science of Hitting (Simon and Schuster, 1971) ↗. His own phrasing is rougher and longer, and it never claims golf is the “only” such sport.
Not a fabricated connection: Golf Digest’s July 1960 cover story ↗ carries his byline on Sam Snead, with Snead writing on him in the same issue. Neither piece is the source of this line.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Williams’s and it is on the record; the sentence is not. Until someone produces a page, a broadcast or a dated newspaper column, the honest attribution is attributed to Ted Williams, source unknown — and the quotable thing he actually wrote is in The Science of Hitting ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks to him anyway
lead: The line survives because it is not really wrong about Ted Williams — it is only wrong about what he said. Williams opened The Science of Hitting by insisting that hitting a baseball is the single most difficult thing to do in sport, and he anticipated the obvious objection himself: somebody always mentions golf. So he took golf apart. You do not need good eyesight for it, he wrote, pointing to the one-eyed Tommy Armour; you do not need speed, or great strength, or youth. Nobody boos. Nothing can hurt you unless lightning strikes. And then the closer — “there’s that golf ball, sitting right there for you to hit, and a flat-faced club to hit it with.”

The one-liner is that whole passage wrung out into fourteen words, and it is the wringing-out that gives it away: Williams argued in paragraphs, with examples and names in them, not in bumper stickers. He was not hostile to the game, either. In July 1960 Golf Digest ran him and Sam Snead on facing bylines, each imagining a career in the other’s sport — Williams writing on Snead, Snead writing on Williams. Nothing resembling the aphorism has turned up in that pairing, in his books, or in the newspaper record.
context.detailsSummary: Why the wording gives itself away
detailsBody: The claim is not even true as stated. Golf is plainly not the only sport played from a ball at rest — a bowler, a pool player and a place-kicker all address a ball that is sitting perfectly still. Williams’s own version never makes the “only sport” claim; it just notes, in passing, that the golf ball is not going anywhere. Somebody later sharpened an observation into a boast, which is how most aphorisms are manufactured.

The circulation footprint is unusually thin as well. Big scraper aggregators normally amplify a fake quote until it is everywhere; this one is largely confined to Wikiquote’s unsourced holding pen and pages that copy from it. That pattern is consistent with a paraphrase that escaped a discussion page, not with a line that ever appeared in print under his name.
context.pull: The thought is his. The sentence is somebody else’s tidying-up.

Baseball Almanac's Ted Williams quote page prints a source beside each quotation and contains no golf quotation.

AZQuotes' Ted Williams page does not list the golf line among the quotations it displays.
The Library of Congress catalogues The Science of Hitting by Ted Williams and John Underwood as New York: Simon and Schuster, [1971], 88 pages, LCCN 79139668.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of The Science of Hitting by Ted Williams and John Underwood, publisher New York: Simon & Schuster, dated 1986 ("A Fireside book").
Golf Digest's July 1960 issue carried the cover story "SAM SNEAD... A king-sized Yogi Berra?" bylined Ted Williams, alongside "TED WILLIAMS... Golf's first southpaw champion?" by Sam Snead.
Ted Williams was born 30 August 1918, died 5 July 2002, hit .406 for the Boston Red Sox in 1941, and served as a Marine combat aviator in the Second World War and the Korean War.

The text of The Science of Hitting opens "Hitting a baseball—I've said it a thousand times—is the single most difficult thing to do in sport" and, in the same chapter, contains "And there's that golf ball, sitting right there for you to hit, and a flat-faced club to hit it with" — no sentence in the book resembles "Golf is the only sport where the ball doesn't move until you hit it."
